summary: Welsh-born journalist Henry Morton Stanley found David Livingstone in 1871, then shot and flogged his way across Central Africa and secured the treaties that let King Leopold II seize the Congo.

evidence.note: born John Rowlands, illegitimate, in Wales; start of the lifetime span
placed in the St Asaph workhouse at six; abuse of child inmates discussed at length
enlists with the Confederate Dixie Grays, fights at Shiloh, later switches to the Union
postwar trip to Anatolia with Louis Noe, violent clash with locals
becomes a reporter on the Indian Wars, then roving correspondent for the Herald
finds Livingstone at Ujiji in November 1871; start of main span
1874-77 expedition traces the Lualaba and Congo, more than half his party dies
host reads long racist passages from Stanley's journals
account of the punitive massacre of the Bambira after a dispute over oars
signs hundreds of sovereignty treaties for Leopold that found the Congo Free State
Emin Pasha relief expedition from 1887, his last African trip; end of main span
Jeal's 2007 rehabilitation and the statue campaign framed in modern empire debates

notes: Tim Jeal, the revisionist biographer, gets as much airtime as many episodes give a secondary subject, so he is listed; his 2007 book and the Denbigh statue campaign are treated as reinterpretation and set reaches_present rather than extending covered_span. Primary theme could equally be colonialism-imperialism; science-exploration chosen per the taxonomy example.
